5. Sample selection and descriptive statistics

Our sample selection process is detailed in Table 1. The sample selection begins with all
COMPUSTAT firm-years between 1993 and 2010 with non-negative sales and asset observations, and nonmissing historical SIC codes. Based on Jan and Ou (2012), we do not
exclude negative book-to-market companies because doing so would induce sample selection bias. This bias arises because firms with significant R&D expenditures may represent
negative book value companies and because R&D expenditures are an input into the
STRATEGY measure, we would omit a large number of potential Prospector firms. We
require five years of data (1988 through 1992) to compute STRATEGY for the first year
(1993) of our sample period. Following Bentley et al. (2013), we require at least three
years of nonmissing observations for our measure to preserve observations, provided that
the company has at least six years of consecutive data in COMPUSTAT. <sup>13</sup> We also
require an additional year (1987) to create lagged variables.

We start with 163,173 firm-years of COMPUSTAT data. This number excludes observations associated with a subsidiary or foreign incorporated unit. We also delete 29,663
firm-year observations associated with firms in financial services and regulated industries


11. Although STRATEGY includes a measure of growth, it does not specifically include the market-to-book
ratio, so we include this control variable. Results are similar if we estimate the model without MtoB.
12. Recent revelations in the press indicate that some firms do not fully disclose their principal affiliates.
Because Prospectors are more aggressive in their financial reporting than Defenders (Bentley et al. 2013),
we suspect that Prospectors are less likely to report principal affiliates on Schedule 21 of the 10-K. This
misclassification should bias against our results.
13. Our inferences remain unchanged if we require firms to have five years of nonmissing data.
